content: In 2011, the age-adjusted prevalence of the disease in the United States was reported as a specific percentage. The delay-adjusted incidence of the disease in 2011 was estimated to be a certain number per 100,000 individuals in the United States. In the same year, the age-adjusted incidence of the disease was calculated as a specific number per 100,000 individuals in the United States. Between 2007 and 2011, the overall age-adjusted incidence of the disease in the United States was a certain number per 100,000 individuals. When broken down by age groups, the age-adjusted incidence was a specific number per 100,000 for individuals under 65 years of age and a different number per 100,000 for those aged 65 and older. In 2011, the age-adjusted prevalence of the disease in the United States was stratified by gender. Among males, the prevalence was a specific percentage, while among females, it was a different percentage. The delay-adjusted incidence of the disease in 2011, when stratified by gender, was a certain number per 100,000 individuals for males and a different number per 100,000 individuals for females. Similarly, the age-adjusted incidence of the disease in 2011, when stratified by gender, was a specific number per 100,000 individuals for males and a different number per 100,000 individuals for females. A visual representation is provided, showing the delay-adjusted and observed incidence of the disease by gender and race in the United States from 1975 to 2011. These graphs are sourced from the SEER (Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results) Program of the National Cancer Institute. A table is presented, illustrating the age-adjusted prevalence of the disease by race in the United States in 2011. Additionally, an image is provided, showing the incidence of the disease by race in the United States from 1975 to 2011. The racial categories include Asian/Pacific Islander (API) and American Indian/Alaska Native (AI/AN). Among patients with histologically confirmed cases of the disease, the percentage distribution of different histological types between 2007 and 2011 in the United States is as follows: Type X accounts for a specific percentage, Type Y for another percentage, and Type Z for a different percentage. Between 2004 and 2010, the 5-year relative survival rate for patients diagnosed with the disease was a specific percentage. When stratified by age, the 5-year relative survival rate was a certain percentage for patients under 65 years of age and a different percentage for those aged 65 years and older. The survival rate of patients with the disease varies depending on the stage of the disease at diagnosis. A table is provided, showing the 5-year relative survival rates by stage of the disease. An image is included, depicting the 5-year conditional relative survival rates (the probability of surviving the next 5 years given that the cohort has already survived 0, 1, or 3 years) between 1998 and 2010. These rates are stratified by the stage of the disease at diagnosis and are based on data from the SEER Program of the National Cancer Institute. The data and visualizations are adapted from the SEER Cancer Statistics Review, 1975-2011, published by the National Cancer Institute in Bethesda, MD, and based on the November 2013 SEER data submission, which was made available on the SEER website in April 2014.
